papers.title: A Deep Learning-Driven Operator Splitting Scheme for Free Boundary Problems: An Application to American Option Pricing in Incomplete Markets
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a deep learning-driven operator splitting scheme for high-dimensional free-boundary problems, with American option pricing as a representative application. In a market with proportional transaction costs, a stochastic liquidity risk with an empirically validated nonlinear drift based on S&P 500 data, and two-factor stochastic volatility, the pricing problem takes the form of a five-dimensional highly nonlinear variational inequality. The proposed scheme decomposes this variational inequality at each time layer into an elliptic continuation equation approximated by a physics-informed neural network and a closed-form projection step enforcing the early-exercise constraint. A conditional $\ell^\infty$ stability bound is derived under stated resolvent and Lipschitz assumptions. The scheme is validated against finite-difference and least-squares Monte Carlo benchmarks, and both the option prices and the learned exercise boundary show close agreement with the reference solutions. Sensitivity analyses with respect to the key model parameters are also reported.

papers.title: An Application of Geometric Riemannian Pricing Algorithm for Valuing Catastrophe Bonds in Incomplete Markets: Market-Consistent Financial Entropy and the Split of Frequency and Severity Risk Premia
papers.abstract: This paper presents a framework for pricing catastrophe (CAT) bonds in incomplete markets through Riemannian geometric optimization of financial entropy. We formulate pricing-measure selection as a maximum financial entropy problem on a finite-dimensional manifold of equivalent measures, parameterized by the non-hedgeable market prices of catastrophe frequency and severity risk, with discounting fixed by the default-free term structure. Since unconstrained entropy maximization recovers the physical measure, we incorporate observed secondary-market spreads, both pooled and date by date. For a compound Poisson-generalized Pareto loss model with Wang distortion, we derive closed-form expressions for financial entropy and the Riemannian metric. We show that CAT bond prices depend on frequency and severity premia primarily through the risk-neutral trigger intensity, making the two premia unidentifiable from market data alone; the entropy criterion resolves this ambiguity. Using a hypothetical earthquake CAT bond calibrated to quarterly spreads of Golden State Re II Ltd. (Series 2014-1), we obtain risk-neutral trigger intensities of 6.58 to 10.45 times the physical intensity (9.20 pooled and 18.26 at the end of 2015). The model-implied risk multiple aligns with the market spread-to-expected-loss ratio (8.87 versus 8.81 at issuance). The minimal-entropy measure attributes 53.5% to 63.7% of the log risk multiple to frequency risk, reflecting the selection principle rather than market identification. Finally, equating the coupon with the quoted spread understates the risk multiple by approximately half.

papers.title: Optimal Order Placement under a State-Dependent Hawkes Process Limit Order Book model
papers.abstract: We study optimal quote placement for a market maker facing order flow modeled by a state-dependent Hawkes process. A block-based linear demand specification links market-order counts to execution volumes, providing the demand moments required by a continuous time discrete state dynamic programming formulation. Under a quadratic terminal inventory penalty, we characterize inventory-dependent quotes and derive backward recursions for the coefficients of a quadratic value function. Numerical experiments using LOBSTER data examine quote distributions, inventory exposure, and terminal wealth. The implemented strategy yields higher aggregate terminal wealth than fixed-spread benchmarks at one and three ticks, but lower wealth than the two-tick benchmark. These results illustrate the framework's numerical implementation and distinguish terminal-wealth comparisons from evaluation under the inventory-penalized objective.

papers.title: Low-rank and graphon limits for dynamic threshold distress contagion in heterogeneous financial networks
papers.abstract: We study how financial distress propagates through a directed network when institutions can recover and become distressed again. Each institution's current buffer determines its loss transmission rate, so the duration of distress affects its creditors' cumulative losses. We show that the dynamics of a network with $K$ sender--receiver factor pairs can be represented exactly by a closed system of $K$ feedback equations. For bounded Lipschitz loss rates, we prove stability with respect to population and exposure changes, using Wasserstein distance for type distributions and aligned norms for kernels. These estimates quantify the error in approximating a directed graphon model by finite factor networks. Hard thresholds introduce a further difficulty: when many institutions lie close to the threshold, the same initial data can admit several contagion paths. For bounded nonnegative kernels and bounded initial profiles, we construct the greatest cumulative-distress solution and show that vanishing positive-side regularization selects it. We prove uniqueness, quantitative stability, and convergence of sampled nonnegative networks under an Osgood condition on the mass near the threshold along a reference solution. Rank-one examples establish sharpness among uniqueness guarantees based only on this mass. Numerical experiments illustrate how recovery interrupts new loss transmission while past losses persist. Using the disclosed sovereign portfolios of 116 banks under prescribed stress scenarios, we also examine how the choice of retained channels affects approximation accuracy. In the baseline scenario, retaining the two most strongly shocked channels gives a maximum buffer-path error about one fifteenth that of a twelve-mode singular-value truncation.
